## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. For any positive integer $n$, there exists a prime $p$ such that the multiplicative order of $d_1 d_2^{-1}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is greater than $n$.

**Setup.** Let $r = d_1/d_2$. We are given $\gcd(d_1, d_2) = 1$ and $r \neq \pm 1$. For a prime $p \nmid d_1 d_2$, the element $r \bmod p = d_1 d_2^{-1} \bmod p$ is well-defined in $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$, and its order is the smallest positive $k$ with $r^k \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, i.e., $d_1^k \equiv d_2^k \pmod{p}$, i.e., $p \mid (d_1^k - d_2^k)$.

**Key observation.** The order of $r \bmod p$ is $\leq n$ if and only if $p$ divides at least one of the integers $d_1^k - d_2^k$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$.

**These integers are nonzero.** Suppose $d_1^k - d_2^k = 0$ for some $k \geq 1$. Then $d_1^k = d_2^k$. Since $\gcd(d_1, d_2) = 1$, we have $d_1^k \mid d_2^k$ forces $|d_1| = 1$, and $d_2^k \mid d_1^k$ forces $|d_2| = 1$. Thus $d_1, d_2 \in \{1, -1\}$, giving $r = d_1/d_2 \in \{1, -1\}$, contradicting $r \neq \pm 1$. Hence $d_1^k - d_2^k \neq 0$ for every $k \geq 1$.

**Finiteness of bad primes.** Define
$$M_n = \prod_{k=1}^{n} (d_1^k - d_2^k).$$
This is a nonzero integer, so it has finitely many prime divisors. Let $S_n$ be the (finite) set of primes dividing $M_n \cdot d_1 \cdot d_2$. Any prime $p \notin S_n$ satisfies $p \nmid d_1 d_2$ (so $r \bmod p$ is defined) and $p \nmid (d_1^k - d_2^k)$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$ (so $r^k \not\equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$).

**Existence of a good prime.** Since there are infinitely many primes and $S_n$ is finite, there exists a prime $p \notin S_n$. For this prime, $r \bmod p \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ has order strictly greater than $n$.

**Conclusion.** For every positive integer $n$, a prime $p$ exists such that $\operatorname{ord}_p(d_1 d_2^{-1}) > n$. $\blacksquare$
